'''''Cerastes''''' is a [[genus]] of small [[Viperinae|viper]]s found in the [[desert]]s and [[Semi-arid region|semi-deserts]] of northern [[North Africa]] eastward through [[Arabian Peninsula|Arabia]] and [[Iran]].<ref name="McD99"/><ref name="SB95"/> Three [[species]] are recognized as being valid by [[Integrated Taxonomic Information System|ITIS]]<ref name="ITIS">{{ITIS |id=634421 |taxon=''Cerastes'' |accessdate=30 July 2006}}</ref> and the [[Reptile Database]].<ref name="RDB">{{EMBL genus|genus=Cerastes}} www.reptile-database.org.</ref> Common names for members the genus include '''horned vipers''',<ref name="Mal03">[[David Mallow|Mallow D]], [[David Ludwig (herpetologist)|Ludwig D]], [[Göran Nilson|Nilson G]] (2003). ''True Vipers: Natural History and Toxinology of Old World Vipers''. Malabar, Florida: Krieger Publishing Company. 359 pp. {{ISBN|0-89464-877-2}}.</ref> '''North African desert vipers''',<ref name="SB95">[[Stephen Spawls|Spawls S]], [[William Roy Branch|Branch B]] (1995). ''The Dangerous Snakes of Africa''. Sanibel Island, Florida: Ralph Curtis Books. 192 pp. {{ISBN|0-88359-029-8}}.</ref> and '''cerastes vipers'''.<ref name="P&G77">[[Hampton Wildman Parker|Parker HW]], [[species:Alice Georgie Cruickshank Grandison|Grandison AGC]] (1977). ''Snakes – a natural history''. (2nd edition). London and Ithaca: British Museum (Natural History) and Cornell University Press. 108 pp. + 16 plates. LCCCN 76-54625. {{ISBN|0-8014-1095-9}} (cloth), {{ISBN|0-8014-9164-9}} (paper).</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Cerastes-cerastes head.jpg|left|thumb|240px|''C. cerastes'', horned individual.]]
''Cerastes'' species are small snakes, averaging less than {{convert|50|cm|in|abbr=on}} in total length (body + tail), but are relatively stout in appearance. The head is broad, flat and distinct from the neck. The head is covered with tubercularly keeled scales, which usually number 15 or more across, and a supraorbital horn may be present over each eye in some species. The snout is short and wide and the eyes, which are set well forward, are small to moderate in size.<ref name="Mal03"/><ref name="SB95"/> The body is short, stout and cylindrically depressed. The tail is short and tapers abruptly behind the vent.<ref name="Mal03"/> The [[dorsal scales]] are small, [[Keeled scales|keeled]], in 23–35 rows at midbody,<ref name="SB95"/> with the keels of the oblique lateral row being serrated.<ref name="Mal03"/>

Although ''Cerastes'' are often referred to as horned vipers, only the two larger species, ''C. cerastes'' and ''C. gasperettii'', are known to have horns, and even these do not always have them. Individuals with and without horns occur within the same population and even within the same litter.<ref name="Mal03"/>

When present, each horn consists of a single long, spine-like scale that can be folded back into an indentation in the [[postocular scale]]. They fold back in response to direct stimulation, thus streamlining the head and easing passage through burrows. Horns occur more often in individuals from sandy deserts as opposed to stony deserts. Specimens without horns have a prominent brow ridge instead.<ref name="Mal03"/>

The purpose of the horns is the subject of much speculation. One theory is that they allow a buildup of sand above the eyes while keeping it out of the eyes themselves.<ref name="Mal03"/> Another, more recent theory is simply that the horns serve to break up the outline of the head, making them harder for prey animals to spot.<ref name="SB95"/>

==Geographic range==
''Cerastes'' species are found in [[North Africa]] eastward through [[Arabian Peninsula|Arabia]] and [[Iran]].<ref name="McD99"/> Mallow et al. (2003) describe the genus as being restricted to the deserts of North Africa and [[Southwest Asia|southwestern Asia]], with the [[Negev|Negev desert]] acting as a filter zone between the three species mentioned in the table below.<ref name="Mal03"/>

==Habitat==
The preferred natural [[habitat]] of ''Cerastes'' species is desert and semi-desert.<ref name="SB95"/>

==Behavior==
[[File:Cerastes vipera.ogv|thumb|Captive cerastes sinking into sand]]
The genus ''Cerastes'' is [[Nocturnality|nocturnal]] and [[Terrestrial animal|terrestrial]] (not known to climb into [[Shrub|bushes]]), often hiding by burying themselves in the sand. Although often described as slow moving, these snakes are also capable of sidewinding. When doing so, they can move quickly across the sand.<ref name="SB95"/>

''Cerastes'' species are not known to be particularly ill-tempered ("fairly placid"), but when threatened they will often stand their ground and form C-shaped coils that are rubbed together to produce a rasping or crackling sound, similar to ''[[Echis]]''. This is called [[stridulation]]. With enough provocation, they will strike from this position.<ref name="Mal03"/><ref name="SB95"/>

These snakes are capable of "sinking" quickly down into loose sand, using their keeled, angled and serrated lateral scales in a rocking motion. This process begins at the tail and moves forward until the entire head is buried and only the eyes and nostrils are exposed. They can bury themselves this way whether in an outstretched or a coiled position.<ref name="Mal03"/>

==Feeding behavior and diet==
''Cerastes'' species are ambush [[Predation|predators]] that lie buried in the sand, waiting for prey to pass by. Their diet consists mainly of [[rodent]]s, [[bird]]s, and [[lizard]]s.<ref name="Mal03"/>

==Reproduction==
All three species of ''Cerastes'' lay [[egg]]s. However, those of ''C. vipera'' hatch within hours of deposition as opposed to many weeks, something not previously observed in other African snakes, most of which lay eggs that hatch weeks later or give birth to live young.<ref name="SB95"/>

In addition to the three above species recognized by "ITIS", ''Cerastes boehmei'' was described in 2010, but has subsequently been synonymized with ''[[Cerastes vipera]]''.<ref>[[Philipp Wagner|Wagner P]], [[species:Thomas M. Wilms|Wilms TM]] (2010). "A crowned devil: new species of ''Cerastes'' Laurenti, 1768 (Ophidia, Viperidae) from Tunisia, with two nomenclatural notes". ''Bonn Zoological Bulletin'' '''57''' (2): 297–306. (''Cerastes boehmei'', new species).</ref><ref>{{EMBL species|genus=Cerastes|species=vipera}} www.reptile-database.org.</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Although it would seem that Laurenti changed his mind in 1768 and decided to name this genus ''Aspis'', instead of ''Cerastes'' as he did earlier, this was eventually rejected. The [[International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature]] (ICZN) later placed the name ''Cerastes'' on the Official List of Generic Names in Zoology (name no. 1539), while the name ''Aspis'' was placed on the Official Index of Invalid Generic Names in Zoology (name no. 1630).<ref name="McD99"/>
